Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Linh had been nine when the kitchen linoleum felt like the whole world. Her father's sudden, sweeping motion had forced her to curl into the corner while her clothes were torn, leaving her feeling utterly exposed and objectified. Years later, any clinical examination or the quiet awareness of being observed by strangers would resurrect that exact sensation of exposure, sending a wave of nausea through her stomach. When she tried to deliberately focus on the event, her mind went blank, the visual details dissolving into a heavy, suffocating pressure. Yet, when the fog lifted enough for her to remember, an intense rage would flood her, hot and sharp. The rage on recall and the image-less panic cemented her negative appraisal that she was a weak person, entirely at the mercy of larger forces. The injustice of it had settled into her bones; nothing had ever been done about it. Because the trauma had stripped her of any sense of bodily autonomy, she now felt like a mere object, her body and needs dismissed as irrelevant. This dehumanizing appraisal, born directly from those early beatings, now dictated how she navigated every new situation. She would instinctively lean in, agreeing to take on extra deadlines or shift her schedule, purely to keep the peace and feel momentarily safe. She also found herself constantly replaying how life would have been different if she had simply been quieter, a counterfactual loop that kept her mentally trapped in the past. By constantly yielding to others' demands, she inadvertently avoided any reminders of bodily exposure or authority figures, which meant she rarely paused to examine what she was actually feeling. Her fragmented memories meant she could not process the trauma, which pushed her toward people pleasing and counterfactual thinking as substitutes for understanding, a maladaptive strategy that kept her trapped. This avoidance of internal processing left her memories difficult to access on purpose, which in turn allowed the raw, image-less emotional intensity of the event to surface unbidden. The constant emotional whiplash convinced her that the world remained an inherently dangerous place, a threat appraisal that solidified whenever she noticed the quiet judgment in a colleague's eyes. Now, as an urban planner, her office became a testing ground for these ingrained patterns. Her apartment was the only place she felt secure; stepping outside meant entering a landscape of unpredictable variables where she had no control. When she toured downtown development sites, her concentration on zoning maps frayed the moment a contractor made a quick, unannounced gesture near her clipboard, putting her immediately on guard. This threat in movements made even routine occupational health exams trigger a wave of nausea. This constant state of threat monitoring made it impossible to trust her own judgment, so she relied entirely on people pleasing to navigate the site tours without drawing attention. This hypervigilance also meant her memories of the kitchen floor remained both too blurry and too violent to bear, so she kept her mind occupied with spreadsheet columns, yet the somatic wave of nausea still arrived unannounced. The physiological alarm felt indistinguishable from the past, reinforcing her dehumanizing belief that she was just a cog in a larger machine. The loop tightened with every site visit. The nausea and fear of being seen became her primary triggers, pulling her back into the people-pleasing habits that had once been her only shield. This people-pleasing meant she avoided reminders of authority, but it also kept her hypervigilant in new settings, where every sudden movement now felt like a trigger. The counterfactual loop she maintained to cope only deepened her sense of threat, making the world feel perpetually unstable. By constantly yielding to others' demands, she inadvertently reinforced her own belief that she lacked the strength to set boundaries, which deepened her sense of injustice and dehumanization. What finally brought her to seek help was a panic attack in the subway, right as the train doors closed with a sudden slam. She was terrified that the memories would finally flood back, that the rage would consume her, but she was also desperate to finally prove to herself that she was not weak, and that the world was not out to erase her.
